title: The Myth of Neutral Education
author: D.P. Curtin
summary: D.P. Curtin argues that the 19th-century aspiration to build neutral, value-free public education is fundamentally impossible. Surveying Greek paideia, Roman civic formation and medieval learning, he shows that every civilization has treated education as the formation of character and the selection of virtue. He locates the confusion in conflating neutrality toward people, which teachers owe, with neutrality toward ideas, which no one can have. Every syllabus and every curriculum embodies a judgment about what is worth knowing, and he cites Newman, Arnold and Babbitt as writers who openly accepted education as moral formation. The Philadelphia Bible Riots of 1844 serve as a historical example of a supposedly neutral practice that was sectarian in effect. His conclusion is that the pretense of neutrality hides moral commitments and weakens democratic accountability, so the honest question is whether educators will admit the moral judgments they make.
points: Neutral education is a modern illusion; every curriculum answers the question of what a well-formed human being looks like.
Neutrality toward students as persons is a duty, but neutrality toward ideas is impossible for any teacher or syllabus.
What schools omit, such as Homer, Augustine or Douglass, reveals their moral priorities as much as what they include.
Institutions that most loudly claim neutrality often have the strongest tacit moral vision, which obscures democratic accountability.
Teaching honesty, diligence and respect for truth is already moral formation, so the task is to be honest about it and avoid propaganda.
quotes: It is only a modern development that has posited the strange conviction that schools can offer knowledge without making judgments about what is good and bad in the world.
Education cannot escape values because education itself is a deliberate act of the selection of virtue. Every curriculum is built upon the sundry judgments about what is worth knowing.
Attempting to create a value-less education is akin to the process of trying to bite your own teeth or stand outside of your own shadow.
The question is not whether values are being taught. Plainly speaking, they are, and have been for quite some time.
Students who complete their formal education without a passing familiarity with Homer, Shakespeare, Augustine, Dante, Tocqueville, or Frederick Douglass have not received a neutral education.

This is all to say, there is no view from nowhere. The frustrating and tragic irony is that institutions that speak most frequently of institutional neutrality often possess the most potent, tacit moral vision.
A school that teaches honesty, diligence, courage, charity, or an abiding respect for truth has already entered the realm of moral formation. There is no escaping this reality, only denying it.
